prompt: Tapping Pause also fires the weapon. Which fix prevents the conflict?
choices: Make the weapon fire more slowly
Give UI touches priority and prevent them reaching gameplay
Use a smaller Pause button
Disable all touch input
explanation: A touch claimed by a UI button should not also fire a gameplay action. Separate UI ownership from world input.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 17: UI and gameplay input

prompt: A diagonal swipe makes a runner change lane and jump. Which rule produces one clear command?
choices: Trigger both axes whenever they move
Require three fingers
Lock the dominant axis after a threshold and accept one command
Wait until the next level
explanation: A runner needs one clear directional command per accepted swipe. Use a movement threshold, choose the dominant direction, and commit once.

prompt: You drag a tower onto an invalid tile. What should happen when you release?
choices: Build it anyway
Hide the tower permanently
Spend currency before checking the tile
Show invalid placement and return or cancel the drag
explanation: Preview snapping, range and valid placement while dragging. Commit on a valid area; otherwise return or cancel clearly.

prompt: A button charges an attack while held. What makes the wait understandable?
choices: Visible charge progress and a clear release rule
No feedback until release
Random charge duration
A smaller button
explanation: Hold needs visible progress and a predictable release or cancellation rule. Otherwise charging can feel like input delay.

prompt: A list item activates while the player starts scrolling. What is the best fix?
choices: Activate every item immediately
Delay activation until the movement stays within tap tolerance
Disable scrolling
Require a double tap for every gesture
explanation: Let movement distinguish a tap from a scroll. The scroll view can claim the drag before the item commits.

prompt: The app loses focus while a player is dragging. What should the input system do?
choices: Keep the finger active forever
Commit the drag at a random position
Clear active ownership and previews safely
Trigger the held action again
explanation: Focus loss, system cancellation and scene changes need a cancellation path that leaves the game in a valid state.

topic: Week 4 · From gesture to game action
prompt: You want Dodge to work from a swipe, keyboard and gamepad. Where should gameplay receive input?
choices: In separate gameplay code for each device
Directly from raw finger coordinates everywhere
Only from the touchscreen
From a named Dodge action shared by the control schemes
explanation: Map different device inputs onto a named game action. This keeps the mechanic independent of the control scheme.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 25: From gesture to game action

topic: Week 4 · Safe areas and display cutouts
prompt: A phone cutout hides the health display. Which layout rule fixes it?
choices: Anchor critical HUD elements inside the safe area
Move every element to the screen center
Shrink all text until it fits
Ignore the cutout in landscape
explanation: Keep critical HUD and touch targets inside safe anchors. Background art may extend beyond them; test both orientations.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 31: Safe areas and display cutouts

prompt: Which layout suits a portrait game intended for one-thumb play?
choices: Movement and aim must be simultaneous on opposite sides
Frequent actions inside one reachable region
Every action requires two fingers
Tiny buttons along the top edge
explanation: One-thumb play needs frequent actions in a reachable region. Avoid assuming two simultaneous controls.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 14: One-thumb and two-thumb play

prompt: Which gesture best suits moving an object continuously with your finger?
choices: A one-time tap
A directional swipe with one command
A drag that shows the object following the finger
A long press with no visual response
explanation: Drag is direct manipulation: the object or camera follows the finger continuously. Preserve a stable finger-to-object offset.

topic: Week 4 · Editor success is incomplete evidence
prompt: The prototype works with a mouse in the editor. What still needs real-device testing?
choices: Nothing; the editor proves touch works
Only the title screen text
Only the level count
Touch identity, display layout, runtime and performance
explanation: Mouse success does not prove multi-touch comfort, safe-area layout, packaging behavior or frame pacing on a phone.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 3: Editor success is incomplete evidence

prompt: Which loop gives useful mobile prototype evidence?
choices: Edit, build, install, run, observe, fix
Only edit until the project is finished
Build once at the end of the course
Watch another team play a different build
explanation: Short device loops expose defects early. Record device, build version, reproduction steps and the expected result.

topic: Week 4 · Android and iOS build paths
prompt: Why keep the package name or bundle identifier stable during development?
choices: It increases frame rate automatically
It preserves the app identity across development builds
It removes the need for touch testing
It changes the device orientation
explanation: The package or bundle identifier defines the app identity. Keep it stable so development builds can replace earlier installations predictably.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 9: Android and iOS build paths

topic: Week 4 · A minimum device test matrix
prompt: Your game works on one phone. What is the most useful next test?
choices: Repeat only the same title screen
Stop testing until release
Use a contrasting screen and test interruptions
Remove all platform logging
explanation: A contrasting screen exposes HUD assumptions. Backgrounding, orientation changes and rapid touch sequences reveal common defects.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 11: A minimum device test matrix

prompt: A gesture needs time to classify. How can the interface still feel responsive?
choices: Commit every gesture immediately before validation
Ignore the finger until classification finishes
Skip visual feedback entirely
Acknowledge the touch immediately, then confirm the validated action
explanation: Show a press state or contact marker on begin, then give distinct feedback when the command commits. Acknowledgement and commitment can be separate.
source: MGD_4_week.pptx · slide 29: Feedback, latency and forgiveness
